editorial:
Imagine making a movie and then having the government just tell you that nobody is allowed to see it. That is exactly what happens to Kenneth Griffith in this fascinating documentary. You get to follow him as he plays detective in his own life, trying to figure out why his films about Michael Collins and Badon Powell were banned. It feels less like a dry history lesson and more like a mystery story. You will meet some huge names along the way, like Peter O'Toole and Morley Safer, who help Griffith dig through the secrets of censorship and power.

What really makes this work is how it shows the fight for free speech without being boring. The interviews are sharp, and seeing Griffith's frustration makes you really root for him. While some of the older footage might feel a bit slow, the curiosity keeps you hooked. If you love true stories about fighting the system, you should definitely check this out.
endingExplained: By the end, Griffith realizes that the banning of his films was not about the quality of the work, but about political fear and control. He manages to expose how the authorities used censorship to hide uncomfortable truths. The movie wraps up by showing that while the fight was long and frustrating, the truth eventually comes out. It leaves you feeling that the public's right to know is more important than any government secret.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves true stories about free speech and political mysteries.
